ds: Individuals, witting or unwitting, whose accounts or identities are used to receive and move criminal proceeds on behalf of others, often recruited via fake job offers, romance scams or social media. Mule activity is a key layering and cash-out step for fraud and other crime proceeds.

FATF, Money Laundering from Fraud typology guidance (general)
FinCEN, advisories on money mule activity (general)

cn.rt: Core consumer typology: mule accounts receive and forward fraud proceeds via digital channels, with handler-accompanied branch and phone contact.

rat: Mule accounts receive and forward funds rapidly, often young or new customers.

ind.n: Inbound third-party payments followed by rapid outbound transfers
ind.cx: Account receives credits from unrelated payers and sends most funds onward within hours or days, retaining a small amount.
ind.fp: Marketplace sellers, agents and family support flows may pass funds on quickly.
ind.ds: Funds received into an account are forwarded onward within a very short period, often in near-equal amounts and leaving minimal balance.

ind.n: New or recently opened account with sudden high activity
ind.cx: Account shows little history then abruptly receives many payments unrelated to the profile.
ind.fp: Students or new arrivals may receive lump sums such as loans or grants.
ind.ds: A recently opened account or newly formed entity with little history abruptly sees large or numerous payments unrelated to its profile.
ind.cn: New account or entity with sudden high activity

ind.n: Account holder profile matches common recruitment demographics
ind.cx: Young, unemployed or newly arrived customers with high flows inconsistent with their stated circumstances.
ind.fp: Profile alone is not suspicious and must not drive discrimination.
ind.ds: Turnover or volumes materially exceed what the customer's declared occupation, income, age or circumstances would support.
ind.cn: Account activity inconsistent with declared occupation or income

ind.n: Customer follows instructions or is coached
ind.cx: In branch or in contact, the customer cannot explain transactions, reads from scripts, or is accompanied by a handler.
ind.fp: Vulnerable or elderly customers may need help for genuine reasons.
ind.ds: Another person speaks for, accompanies or dictates instructions to the customer, who may appear fearful, scripted or unable to explain the activity.
ind.cn: Customer accompanied, directed or coached by a third party

ind.n: Shared devices, IP addresses or contact details across accounts
ind.cx: Multiple unrelated accounts share devices, phone numbers, email or addresses.
ind.fp: Households and shared workplaces share details.
ind.ds: Multiple unrelated accounts share devices, phone numbers, email or addresses.

ind.cx: Inbound payments with references typical of fraud, e.g. invoice, loan fee, investment or romance context.
ind.ds: Payment narratives or references contain wording linked to scams such as safe accounts or investment schemes.

ind.n: Account credentials accessed from remote locations or by third parties
ind.cx: Logins from foreign IPs or remote-access tools soon after opening.
ind.fp: Travel and VPN use are common.
ind.ds: Logins from foreign IPs or remote-access tools soon after opening.

ind.n: International transfers or cryptocurrency purchases following credits
ind.cx: Funds exit via overseas transfers, gift cards or crypto purchases after receipt.
ind.fp: International students and migrants send money abroad.
ind.ds: Incoming funds are quickly sent abroad or converted to virtual assets soon after being credited.
ind.cn: Rapid movement offshore or to crypto after receipt

ind.n: Multiple accounts opened for same individual or by same agent
ind.cx: One person or intermediary opens accounts at several institutions or products.
ind.ds: The same individual appears under different names or opens several accounts or wallets, directly or through an intermediary.
ind.cn: One person holding multiple identities or accounts

ctl.n: Funds hold, freeze and recall procedure
ctl.ds: Provides a defined, legally grounded capability to restrict, hold, freeze or recall funds and accounts pending review or on confirmed exposure, with clear triggers and approvers. It stops onward dissipation of suspected illicit funds.
Model that scores inbound-then-outbound pass-through, new-payee churn, counterparty diversity and profile mismatch to flag likely mule accounts. It prioritises accounts for review and restriction.

Caps transaction size, frequency, load, withdrawal and deposit values, with staged increases as legitimate behaviour is established and per-customer limits at kiosks. It bounds the loss and laundering capacity of new or higher-risk accounts.

ctl.n: Tightened monitoring for new accounts and entities
ctl.ds: Applies lower thresholds and closer review during the first months of an account or entity and alerts on turnover far above onboarding projections. It addresses the elevated risk at the start of a relationship.

Documents that profile attributes alone are never grounds for adverse action and provides guidance supporting legitimate activity, such as humanitarian flows, instead of blanket exits. It limits unfair outcomes and bias in control design.

Compares actual activity with the customer's declared profile, history and peers and alerts on material or trend-breaking deviation, usually as a contextual signal. It catches change that rules on fixed thresholds miss.

Trains branch, contact-centre and relationship staff to ask open questions, recognise coaching, coercion, pressure and evasion and escalate with authority to pause. It strengthens the human control at the point of contact.

Provides discreet escalation routes and private conversation procedures so staff can refer suspected victims of exploitation, coercion or trafficking to specialists, police and support organisations. It prioritises victim safety.

Investigates linked clusters and networks of accounts as one case, including broker networks and accounts connected to seizures or requests, rather than reviewing accounts individually. It disrupts organised activity that single-account review would miss.
Clusters customers, vendors and entities that share addresses, phones, devices, officers or bank details, including against staff records. It reveals common control and hidden relationships.

Matches accounts, devices, identifiers and beneficiaries against industry fraud sharing and ingests law-enforcement, commercial and open-source threat feeds, including victim reports from other institutions. It catches known bad actors early.

Screens payment instructions, references and narrative fields for restricted parties, goods, places and concealment language using tuned matching logic. It catches exposure that does not appear in the customer record.
Analyses typing, navigation, remote-access tooling, call-in-progress signals and deviation from baseline to spot coached, scripted or hijacked sessions. It detects coercion and takeover.
Requires phishing-resistant authentication and additional verification on risky sessions, credential or payee changes and large payments. It blocks unauthorised access and payments.
Verifies instructions, detail changes and unusual requests by contacting the customer on a channel held on file, never one supplied in the request. It defeats impersonation and account takeover.
Alerts when inflows are quickly moved out with little retained balance, including cash-in fast-out and rapid conversion or cash-out. It reveals accounts used as conduits for layering.

ctl.n: Duplicate and synthetic identity checks at onboarding
ctl.ds: Compares new applicant identifiers such as name, email, phone, address, device and bank account with existing customers, previously declined or exited applicants and known-bad data. Matches are blocked or referred, limiting repeat applicants, synthetic identities and mule recruitment.
